transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-28
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Nina (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Park (Sapphire CMO), James O'Neill (Head of IT), Priya Singh (Compliance), Aaron Li (ML Engineer)

---- Summary: ----
Sapphire Clinic is evaluating Redwood for on-prem private inference in a strongly regulated healthcare environment. Primary concerns: offline/airgapped update process (signed firmware/artifacts), limited outbound bandwidth, older GPU hardware inventory, weekly maintenance windows, and auditability (SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM logs, SOC2 artifacts). Team is leaning toward Hosted for sandboxing but requires Private/on-prem for any PHI workloads. Next steps are doc handoff, perf estimates, and a security deep-dive.

---- Topics covered: ----
- Current inference stack and constraints
- Update cadence and approved delivery channels (USB vs sealed media courier)
- Firmware signing, artifact verification, and attestation
- Hardware compatibility (older 16GB GPUs, 4U chassis)
- Audit logs, KMS integration, and SSO requirements
- Pilot scope and timeline

---- Transcript body (timestamps approximated) ----
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Maya, the AE on the account, and Carlos and Nina are our SEs who will lead the technical scoping.
[00:18] Dr. Elena: Hi, thanks. We're keen to understand how Redwood could work in our on-prem environment. Patient data can't leave network, that's the main constraint.
[00:30] James (Head of IT): Yep, and to add, we run in a semi-airgapped mode. Internet is extremely limited — generally only for approved maintenance windows, and most of our updates are done by physical media or an approved courier.
[00:45] Carlos (Redwood SE): Got it. That's a common pattern. Quick question: for initial proof-of-concept, do you have any tolerance for a time-limited outgoing link or is it strictly zero egress?
[01:00] James: For dev sandbox we can open a temporary VPN tunnel but prod is zero egress.
[01:08] Priya (Compliance): And any patch or update must be traceable — signed packages, checksum verification, and a verifiable chain of custody. We need audit logs that show who triggered the update and when.
[01:22] Nina (Redwood SE): Understood. We support an airgapped update flow: signed artifact bundles that can be transported via USB or secure media. Our private package includes a signature manifest and a verification tool.
[01:33] Aaron (ML Eng): When you say signed artifacts, is the verification strictly on the host, or does it call back to Redwood for attestation? We can't have callbacks in prod.
[01:42] Carlos: Good question — for fully airgapped we provide an offline verification binary that verifies signatures against a public key you store in your HSM or KMS. No outbound call-backs required. There is also an optional remote attestation path if you want cloud-backed verifications during non-prod.
[02:05] Dr. Elena: What about key management? We use an on-prem HSM (Thales). We can't export private keys.
[02:13] Maya: We integrate with customer-managed KMS/HSM for key wrapping and storage. Redwood never holds your private signing key for airgapped artifacts. We can support PKCS#11 workflow.
[02:24] Priya: Good. We will need the exact list of audit fields captured in logs — identity, fingerprint of artifact, signature chain, user who initiated, tstamp, and hardware serial numbers.
[02:36] Carlos: We'll share our audit log specimen. It includes timestamp, userID, agentID, artifact hash, and a signed event. Important note: our event schema can be sent as a flat file for ingestion into your SIEM.
[02:50] James: Another practical question — our fleet is older: 2x 16GB GPUs (unknown precise gen), in 2U chassis; power and cooling are constrained. What's the expected footprint?
[03:03] Carlos: We'll need your exact models to give a tight estimate, but generally older 16GB cards will run smaller open models (we can provide quantized variants). For high throughput you may need to shard across several nodes. For example, a single A10-ish card (16GB) with int8 quantization can handle X tokens/sec — we'll quantify after we get inventory.
[03:30] Aaron: We're currently running a CPU fallback for some pipelines; latency must be sub-second for triage tasks. Can Redwood meet that on our hardware?
[03:40] Nina: Sub-second depends on model and sequence length. For short prompts and smaller tuned models we can be in the 200-800ms range with right batch sizing. But on older GPUs you'll need modest batch sizes and lower token windows. We'll include a performance matrix in the follow-up.
[04:00] Maya: Quick qualification — what's the primary success metric for this project? Is it compliance-first, or latency/perf?
[04:08] Dr. Elena: Compliance first. If we can demonstrate secure, auditable inference without PHI leaving network, then we can trade on perf later.
[04:18] Priya: Timeline wise, compliance committee meets first week of May — we'd like a pilot up and running before then to show the board. So roughly a 4-6 week plan.
[04:30] Maya: That's helpful. We can scope a 30-day pilot at one clinic node.
[04:36] Carlos: A few more technical items: offline updates — do you allow USB-inserted media at the data center, or do you only accept sealed courier packages?
[04:46] James: We accept sealed media via courier. USBs are allowed but must be scanned and signed in a secure staging area — it's a pain but doable.
[04:56] Carlos: Okay. Our recommended pattern for airgap is: 1) Redwood provides signed tarball with signature manifest; 2) You stage and scan in staging environment; 3) On approval, ops run the local verifier binary which checks signatures against your stored public key; 4) Update agent applies changes and logs event to local audit store.
[05:20] Dr. Elena: Is the update agent persistent? We worry about a long-lived agent that could be abused.
[05:27] Nina: The agent runs in a least-privileged mode and only executes signed manifests. It can be configured to run only during approved maintenance windows and accepts only one-time tokens for upgrades if you prefer ephemeral triggers.
[05:42] Priya: For one-time tokens, how are those generated and audited?
[05:46] Carlos: They can be generated by your SSO provider or by Redwood's console — for airgapped we recommend generating the token in a vault and then printing/store in your local KMS. We'll document the process.
[06:00] Aaron: Another constraint — our network is flat and doesn't allow pods to reach internal metadata services. Will Redwood install any sidecars that assume cloud metadata?
[06:10] Nina: No, our private deployment can run without metadata services. We support a purely static config mode where all env and secrets are provided during install, and we can run without cloud dependencies.
[06:20] James: Hardware lifecycle — do you support signed firmware updates for the model runtime kernels? Sometimes kernel updates require vendor firmware updates.
[06:28] Carlos: Kernel and runtime updates are bundled as part of the artifact. For firmware that is vendor-specific (BIOS, GPU firmware) we don't push those; we supply guidance and compatibility notes. For our runtime we use reproducible builds and sign binaries; the verification steps are included.
[06:50] Dr. Elena: Ok, we need to know which OS families are supported — we run RHEL7 on some hosts, and Ubuntu 18.04 on others.
[06:58] Nina: We support RHEL7+ and Ubuntu 18.04/20.04. For older distros we might need to ship a containerized runtime. We'll note compatibility caveats.
[07:10] Maya: Let's talk about observability — what logs and metrics are available locally?
[07:15] Carlos: Locally we provide per-request logs (masked by default), token counts, latency histograms, kernel usage, and audit events. We can push metrics to your Prometheus endpoint within the private network, or export flat files for ingestion. No outbound telemetry unless you opt into hosted telemetry during non-prod.
[07:36] Priya: For audit purposes we need tamper-evident logs and WORM storage for audit artifacts for a year. Can Redwood produce logs suitable for WORM archiving?
[07:45] Nina: Yes, logs are printable to append-only files and can be moved to your WORM-enabled storage. The event signatures allow you to validate integrity later.
[07:56] Aaron: On the perf side, what about KV cache — we saw mention of KV cache in docs; does that require any shared filesystem?
[08:03] Carlos: The KV cache can be local to the node or shared over an internal networked cache like Redis; for airgapped we recommend local per-node persistence with optional pre-warmed caches shipped as part of the artifact. Note: sometimes our transcript showed 'KV cash' in old notes — ignore that, it's KV cache.
[08:22] James: Good to clarify. Another question — if we ever decide to move to Dedicated or Hosted in future, how much rework is needed?
[08:30] Maya: We designed the runtime and API to be consistent across Hosted/Dedicated/Private. Rollouts and model pins are config-driven, so migrating to Redwood-hosted services requires minimal config changes and model re-pinning. We'll provide a migration checklist.
[08:45] Dr. Elena: About data retention — we store PHI for 7 years in our EMR; inference logs may be shorter. What's Redwood's retention policy in Private?
[08:55] Carlos: In Private deployments retention is controlled by you. The default config keeps request logs for 30 days unless configured to archive.
[09:03] Priya: For the pilot we need a design doc that outlines compliance controls mapped to our regulator's checklist.
[09:09] Maya: We'll produce a compliance mapping doc. We'll also send a sample runbook for offline updates and the artifact signing runbook.
[09:18] Nina: Any questions on cost model? For Private we typically do a license + support fee and an optional reserved capacity for Dedicated.
[09:26] James: We care more about predictable ops cost; can you provide a per-node license model and then separate maintenance support tiers?
[09:33] Maya: Yes. We'll send a preliminary commercial template.
[09:37] Aaron: For the POC, what's the minimum footprint? One 2U rack with two GPUs?
[09:42] Carlos: For a basic functional POC you can start with one node 2x16GB GPUs for low QPS tests. For production throughput you'll likely want 2-4 nodes. We'll make a sizing doc.
[09:54] Dr. Elena: Ok that sounds reasonable.
[09:58] Maya: Quick recap of next steps before we run out of time?
[10:02] Priya: We're expecting the SOC2 pack and the artifact signing details, and we want a security deep-dive scheduled within a week.
[10:09] James: And hardware inventory and network diagram from our side.
[10:12] Maya: Great. Carlos will also run perf estimates and we'll produce a pilot plan.
[10:17] Carlos: I'll also include a risk list for older GPUs and recommended mitigations.
[10:20] Dr. Elena: Thanks — we'll loop in procurement once compliance signs off.
[10:25] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and a proposed calendar invite for the security deep-dive.
[10:32] (meeting ends)
